citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
Direct and frequent communication with the attending veterinarian regarding the possum’s pacing behavior did not occur.
Per a facility representative, “Joey” the possum developed abnormal pacing once placed in his new enclosure during the
months of February and March of this year. The facility utilized different enrichment methodologies and explained that his
behavior greatly improved. When reviewing records at the time of inspection, 13 incidents of pacing-like behavior, in
varying degrees of significance, were found in the facility’s internal log. The attending veterinarian was not aware of the
possum’s abnormal pacing in those first two months nor was she aware of the ongoing pacing-like behaviors. Veterinary
consultation regarding behavioral problems is necessary to ensure appropriate diagnosis and treatment to minimize
animal distress. A mechanism of direct and frequent communication is required so that timely and accurate information on
problems of animal health, behavior, and well-being is conveyed to the attending veterinarian. Correct by 08/28/2026.

At the time of inspection, three raptors were in indoor enclosures that did not provide enough space for adequate freedom
of movement. The birds were housed in stainless steel veterinary caging that did not allow them to fully extend their wings
without touching enclosure walls or make normal postural adjustments such as changing perches. Per the facility:
- A great horned owl was housed indoors for 4 days while repairs were made in his outdoor enclosure.
- A black vulture was housed indoors for a few days to prevent heat stress from extreme heat temperatures outdoors.
- A broad winged hawk was housed indoors also for a few days because she was not eating well while in her outdoor
enclosure.
The attending veterinarian was not aware that these birds were housed in these enclosures when indoors and for the
hawk as well as the vulture there was no veterinary documentation for the reason and recommended duration of the
restriction.
Primary enclosures that do not allow enough space for adequate freedom of movement can cause stress and discomfort
to the birds and may eventually lead to negative health impacts. Veterinary consultation is necessary to determine the
adequacy of all enclosures used for housing birds regardless of the length of time. Both part-time and full-time attending
veterinarians at a facility must consult with the facility to ensure that the space in all enclosures housing birds is adequate
and allows for normal postural and social adjustments. The normal postural and social adjustments may be restricted only
for 1 of the 4 following reasons given certain standards outlined in the regulations: 1) Veterinary exemption with
documentation of the reason and duration of the restriction, 2) tethering in accordance with current professionally
accepted standards, 3) breeding, 4) transportation. Correct by 09/11/2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
